t:
(a) In General.—The Secretary may carry out projects under section 205 of the Flood Control Act of 1948 (33 U.S.C. 701s), including planning, design, construction, and monitoring of structural and nonstructural technologies and measures, for preventing and mitigating flood damages associated with ice jams. 
    (b) Inclusion.—The projects described in subsection (a) may include the development and demonstration of cost-effective technologies and designs developed in consultation with—
        (1) the Cold Regions Research and Engineering Laboratory of the Corps of Engineers; 
        (2) universities; 
        (3) Federal, State, and local agencies; and 
        (4) private organizations.  
    (c) Pilot Program.—
        (1) In general.—During fiscal years 2017 through 2022, the Secretary shall identify and carry out not fewer than 10 projects under this section to demonstrate technologies and designs developed in accordance with this section. 
        (2) Project selection.—The Secretary shall ensure that the projects are selected from all cold regions of the United States, including the Upper Missouri River Basin and the Northeast.

fable.w: The section contemplates that technologies and designs used in federal ice-jam flood projects are developed in consultation with universities, State and local agencies, and private organizations, all of which are outside the federal government. The tempting "No" reading is that this is only technical collaboration, or intra-federal coordination with the Corps laboratory, and that "may" makes it optional. That reading fails because the list expressly includes non-federal parties whose input shapes the designs the Secretary selects and carries out, and discretionary consultation still counts.

opus.w: This section lets the Secretary develop the technologies and designs for federal ice-jam flood-control projects in consultation with universities, State and local agencies, and private organizations, all of which are outside the federal government. Because these designs feed into the projects the Secretary selects and builds, outsiders are taking part in a federal decision. Example 3 is different because there the outside experts only helped with a study. The Corps laboratory and federal agencies on the list are inside the government, but the outside consultees are enough to answer Yes.
opus.b:
**Tempting wrong reading:** This looks like Example 3, where consulting outside experts on the contents of a study did not count. It also looks like consultation over technical research rather than a policy decision.

**Why it fails:** The consultation here is not about writing a report. It shapes how the Secretary designs the federal flood-control projects actually built under this section. Three of the four listed consultees are outside the federal government: universities, State and local agencies, and private organizations. So outsiders are involved in a federal decision, which meets the definition.
